items.t: Chapter 4 (al-bāb al-rābiʿ) [39]: On an account of the twelve zodiacal signs and the indications and bindings that belong to them

Know — may God, exalted is He, grant success to me and to you in obedience to Him — that I shall set down for you a table before the discussion of the twelve zodiacal signs, in which I shall mention the four seasons, namely spring, summer, autumn, and winter; and I shall mention the twenty-eight lunar mansions in another manner, and the twelve zodiacal signs, and the Arabic months, and the occult properties (khawāṣṣ) that attach to them. God, exalted is He, has said: And indeed We have set constellations in the heaven and adorned it for those who behold (Q 15:16). And God, exalted is He, has said: Blessed is He who set constellations in the heaven (Q 25:61). And God, blessed and exalted is He, has said: By the heaven possessed of the constellations (Q 85:1). I say: burūj is one and the same word — the burūj (constellations) of the heaven, and the burūj of a fortress, which are its corner-tower; and sometimes the fortress itself is named by it. God, exalted is He, has said: even though you were in towers raised high (Q 4:78). And al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī — may God, exalted is He, be pleased with him — said: the burūj are the palaces in the heaven; they are palaces like the palaces of the earth. And God knows best. So understand. And this is the description of the table:
[Table as in the source (): 12 rows × 4 columns, read right to left — month, zodiacal sign, lunar mansion, lunar mansion. No header row in the source.]
Month Zodiacal sign Mansion Mansion
Ādhār (March) al-Ḥamal al-Rishāʾ al-Sharaṭayn (Aries)
Nīsān (April) al-Thawr al-Thurayyā al-Muʾakhkhar (Taurus)
Ayyār (May) al-Jawzāʾ al-Haqʿa al-Buṭayn (Gemini)
Ḥazīrān (June) al-Saraṭān al-Dhirāʿ al-Dabarān (Cancer)
Tammūz (July) al-Asad (Leo) al-Jabha al-Hanʿa
Āb (August) al-Sunbula al-Ṣarfa al-Ṭarf (Virgo)
Aylūl al-Mīzān al-Simāk Kharsān (September) (Libra)
Tishrīn the First al-ʿAqrab al-Iklīl al-ʿAwwāʾ (October) (Scorpio)
Tishrīn the al-Qaws al-Shawla al-Zubānā Second (Sagittarius) (November)
Kānūn the First al-Jady al-Balda al-Qalb (December) (Capricorn)
Kānūn the al-Dālī al-Suʿūd al-Naʿāʾim Second (Aquarius) (January)
Shubāṭ al-Ḥūt (Pisces) al-Muqaddam Balaʿ (February)

Some of the learned have said, concerning His words, exalted is He, Blessed is He who set constellations in the heaven (Q 25:61), that they are the mansions of the seven wandering planets, and they are twelve signs: al-Ḥamal (Aries), al-Thawr (Taurus), al-Jawzāʾ (Gemini), al-Saraṭān (Cancer), al-Asad (Leo), al-Sunbula (Virgo), al-Mīzān (Libra), al-ʿAqrab (Scorpio), al-Qaws (Sagittarius), al-Jady (Capricorn), al-Dalw (Aquarius), and al-Ḥūt (Pisces). Aries and Scorpio are the house of Mars; Taurus and Libra are the house of Venus; Gemini and Virgo are a house for Mercury; Cancer is a house for the Moon; /fol. 21v./ Leo is a house for the Sun; Sagittarius and Pisces are a house for

Jupiter; and Capricorn and Aquarius are a house for Saturn. These signs are divided among the four natures, so that the portion of each one of them is three signs; and they are called the triplicities (al-muthallathāt). Aries, Leo, and Sagittarius are a fiery triplicity; Taurus, Virgo, and Capricorn are an earthy triplicity; Gemini, Libra, and Aquarius are an airy triplicity; and Cancer, Scorpio, and Pisces are a watery triplicity.

The people of Qurʾānic exegesis have differed as to the meaning of al-burūj. Some of them said: they are palaces in which are the guards; and the proof of this is His words, exalted is He, even though you were in towers raised high (Q 4:78). It has been said: they are the stars. And it has been said: they are the lamps, and they are the gates of the heaven which are called the Milky Way (al-majarra). I say: Ibn ʿAbbās — may God, exalted is He, be pleased with them both — has stated expressly that they are the well-known signs to which we have pointed, and that they are twelve signs; and that God, exalted is He, apportioned them into quartiles (tarābīʿ) and trines (tathālīth); and they are divided among the seven planets, as we have mentioned. Every nation names them in its own tongue, yet they agree upon the meaning, and all of them begin with Aries, in the order mentioned. The first sign is Aries. Aries is thirteen stars, and those outside the figure are five stars. Its figure is the figure of a ram, its fore-part toward the quarter of the west and its hind-part toward the east; and it is turned back upon itself, so that its muzzle has come to lie upon its back.

The second sign is Taurus. It is thirty-three stars, and those outside the figure are eleven stars. It is in the figure of the fore-half of a bull, which has lowered its head to butt, and it has been cut into two halves at its navel; its fore-part is toward the east and its hind-part toward the west. Among its stars are al-Thurayyā (the Pleiades) and al-Dabarān (Aldebaran), and these two are lunar mansions.

The third sign is al-Tawʾamān (the Twins), which is known as al-Jawzāʾ (Gemini). It is eighteen stars, and those outside the figure are seven stars. Its figure is two boys standing, one of whom has laid his hand upon the shoulder of the other; their heads and the rest of their stars are in the north and the east, at the edge of the Milky Way, and their feet toward the west.

The fourth sign is Cancer. It is seven stars, and those outside the figure are four stars. Its fore-part is toward the region of the east, and its hind-part toward the region of the west and the south, following upon the Twins, as though the two of them were inclining toward the south, within the Milky Way itself.
The fifth sign is Leo. It is twenty-seven stars, and those outside the figure are eight stars. Its figure is upright. Among its stars is Qalb al-Asad (Regulus, "the Lion's Heart"), a brilliant star.

The sixth sign is al-Sunbula (Virgo, "the Ear of Grain"), and it is known as al-ʿAdhrāʾ (the Virgin). It is twenty-six stars, and those outside the figure are six stars. Its figure is the figure of a maiden with two wings who has let down her train; her head is upon al-Ṣarfa, which is a brilliant star. And among its stars is al-Simāk al-Aʿzal (Spica), which is a brilliant star upon her left shoulder.
The seventh sign is Libra. It is eight stars, and its figure is as its name; and those outside the figure are nine stars.

The eighth sign is /fol. 22r./ Scorpio: twenty-one stars, and those outside the figure are three stars. Its figure is upright. And among its stars is Qalb al-ʿAqrab (Antares, "the Scorpion's Heart"), which is a brilliant star.

The ninth sign is Sagittarius, and it is called al-Rāmī (the Archer). It is thirty-one stars, behind the stars of Scorpio. Its figure is the figure of an animal compounded of a man and a horse: as though it were the body of a beast up to the neck, and then, from the place where the neck divides off, there issues the half of a man who has set the arrow to his bow and drawn it to the utmost, sunk deep in the saddle.

The tenth sign is Capricorn. It is twenty-eight stars, and it is in the figure of the fore-half of a kid, the second half being the hind-part of a fish down to its tail. The eleventh sign is al-Dalw (Aquarius), and it is known as Sākib al-Māʾ (the Pourer of Water). It is forty-two stars, and those outside the figure are three stars. Its figure is the figure of a man standing, stretching out both his hands, in one of them a jug which he has overturned, so that the water pours down toward the fore-part of his feet, and the water runs from beneath it toward the south. It is also called al-Dālī.

The twelfth sign is the sign of Pisces. It is thirty-four stars, and those outside the figure are four stars. Its figure is the figure of two fishes, the tail of the one of which is joined to the tail of the other.

So these twelve signs are three hundred stars — and it has been said, three hundred and forty. And Aries is the first of the signs; and Taurus is a sign in the heaven; and al-Jawzāʾ is a star, of which it is said that it lies athwart the heaven as far as its middle — and the jawz of anything is its middle. And Cancer is a sign in the heaven; but he did not mention Leo. And Virgo is a sign in the heaven; and some of them did not mention Libra. And Scorpio is a sign in the heaven, and likewise Sagittarius, Capricorn, Aquarius, and Pisces. And some of them said that they are signs in the heaven. And al-Jady is a star beside the Pole, by which the qibla is known.
Faṣl: on the lands that belong to each sign

Know that to Aries belong Babylon, Persia, and Azerbaijan; and to Taurus, the land of Hamadhān and the Kurds; and to Gemini belong Jurjān, Kīlān, and Mūqān; and to Cancer belongs the land of China and the eastern part of Khurāsān; and to Leo belong the Turks, the Sughd, and the lands adjoining them; and to Virgo belong Syria, the Jazīra, the Tigris, and the Euphrates; and to Libra belongs the land of Rūm as far as Ifrīqiya, and Upper Egypt, and Abyssinia; and to Scorpio belong the Ḥijāz, the Yemen, and what adjoins them; and to Sagittarius belongs Baghdad as far as Iṣfahān; and to Capricorn, the river of Makrān, and ʿUmān, and Bahrain, and India; and to Aquarius belongs Kūfa as far as the land of the Ḥijāz; and to Pisces belongs Ṭabaristān, and it has a share in Rūm, the Jazīra, Egypt, and Alexandria. We have already mentioned something concerning the climes and what adjoins them, for the sake of completing the discussion of the zodiacal signs. And God knows best.
Faṣl: on the division of time, which is four divisions

The first division is al-rabīʿ (spring), which with some people is al-kharīf (autumn). The Arabs named it rabīʿ only because the rabʿ occurs in it; and some named it kharīf because the fruits are gathered (tukhraf) in it. Its entry is when the sun alights /fol. 22v./ at the head of Libra. Then al-shitāʾ (winter), and its entry is when the sun alights at the head of Capricorn. Then al-ṣayf, and its entry is when the sun alights at the head of Aries — and this with [common] people is the spring. Then al-qayẓ (the hot season), which with [common] people is the summer, and its entry is when the sun alights in Cancer.
Faṣl: on the winds and the discussion concerning them

The first of them is the north wind (al-shamāl), which is the one that blows from the quarter of the Pole. The second of them is al-ṣabā (the east wind), and its place of blowing is the point of equality at the rising of the sun, when night and day are equal. And beneath it is al-dabūr (the west wind). The Arabs allege that al-dabūr stirs up the cloud and beats it down in the air, then drives it along; and when it has been uncovered, and al-ṣabā meets it face to face, then it lays part of it upon part until it becomes one dense mass. And al-janūb (the south wind) brings up its trailing parts to join it and reinforces it, while al-shamāl tears the cloud apart. And the fourth of them is al-janūb, which is the one that blows opposite to al-shamāl; and al-dabūr is the wind that is opposite to al-ṣabā.
Faṣl: on what lies between each heaven and the next

We have already mentioned the doctrine of the ancients concerning the figure of the celestial spheres and what pertains to them. But as for the doctrines of the men of the revealed Law — with them these are "the heavens". Reports have been transmitted on this head from Ibn ʿAbbās — may God, exalted is He, be pleased with him — though it is said [rather] al-ʿAbbās ibn ʿAbd al-Malik. He said: ((We were sitting with the Prophet — God bless him and grant him peace — at al-Baṭḥāʾ, when a cloud passed by. The Prophet — God bless him and grant him peace — said: "Do you know what this is?" We said: "The cloud (al-saḥāb)." He said: "And al-muzn." We said: "And al-muzn." He said: "And al-ʿanān." We said: "And al-ʿanān" — and we fell silent. Then the Prophet — God bless him and grant him peace — said: "Do you know how much lies between the heaven and the earth?" We said: "God and His Messenger know best." He said: "Between them is a journey of five hundred years; and between each heaven and the next is a journey of five hundred years; and the thickness of each heaven — that is to say, its depth — is five hundred years. And above the seventh heaven is a sea, between whose upper part and its lower part is as much as is between the heaven and the earth. Then above that are eight mountain-goats (awʿāl), and [between their knees] and their hooves is as much as is between the heaven and the earth. And God, exalted is He, is above that, and nothing of the deeds of the sons of Adam is hidden from Him.")) And the proof of it is His words, exalted is He: It is God who created seven heavens, and of the earth the like of them (Q 65:12). So the distance of the whole is fourteen thousand years, apart from what is in the heavens of the veils, and the Footstool (al-kursī), and the Throne (al-ʿarsh). And this is according to the measure of the travelling of the sons of Adam. As for the angel, he pierces through the whole of it in a single hour, and some of them in a single instant; and likewise Satan in the earth does what the angel does in the heaven. And Abū Rākima related from ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib — may God be pleased with him and ennoble his face — that he was asked how much lies between [the earth and] the heaven, and he said: "An answered supplication." It was said to him: "And how much lies between the east and the west?" He said: "A journey of a day, for him who obeys his Master" — or, it is said, "a single step", as it has been said: "This world is the step of a believer." And al-Thaʿlabī reported from Ibn ʿAbbās — may God, exalted is He, be pleased with them both — that he said: The sun rises each year through three hundred and sixty apertures, and it does not return to the aperture of that /fol. 23r./ day until the following year.

I say: in the sun there are benefits and indications. Among them is that it is one, and its light shines upon all the horizons and upon the whole world; likewise the Maker (al-Bāriʾ), glorified and exalted is He, is one, and He it is who governs the world. The second: that the sun is far from us while its light is near; likewise God, glorified and exalted, is far from creation in His essence, near in His answering [of prayer]. The third: that its light is withheld from no one; likewise the provision of God, exalted is He, is not withheld from anyone. The fourth: that its eclipse is an indication of the coming of the Resurrection, and its setting indicates the darkness thereof. The fifth: that the clouds cover it; and likewise acts of disobedience are a covering over gnosis. As for its benefits, they are many. Among them: that it is the lamp of the world. God, exalted is He, said: And We made the sun a lamp (Q 71:16). The second: that it is a cook for their foods without trouble, and a ripener of their fruit. The third: that it travels from the east to the west for their welfare. The fourth: that it does not stand still in a single place, lest it harm the creatures. The fifth: that in winter it is in the lowest of the zodiacal signs and in summer in the highest of them, for the benefit of the world. The sixth: that it is not conjoined with the moon in the moon's dominion, lest each of the two annul the light of the other. If it be said: it is in the fourth sphere — why, then, do the heavens not veil it, while the cloud does veil it? — we say: because the heavens are subtle, translucent substances, whereas the cloud is dense, since it rises up out of the earth.
Faṣl: On the moon, the similitudes drawn from it, and what it contains

On the authority of Abū Hurayra — may God, exalted is He, be pleased with him — who said: ((The people said, "O Messenger of God, shall we see our Lord on the Day of Resurrection?" So he — God bless him and grant him peace — said, "Do you dispute about the moon on the night of the full moon, when there is no cloud beneath it?" They said, "No." He said, "And do you dispute about the sun, when there is no cloud beneath it?" They said, "No." Then the Prophet — God bless him and grant him peace — said, "Then indeed you shall see Him just so.")) If it be said: why, then, was the similitude not struck with the sun, since it is more radiant and more complete in light — for the light of the moon is from it? — the answer is from several aspects. The first of them: that the light of the sun overpowers the eyes, so that one is not able to look, and thus the intended purpose is missed; unlike the moon, for the eyes are able to look upon it. And that is because whoever has been broken for the sake of the Truth, blessed and exalted is He, He mends him again. And that is: when Gabriel effaced the light of the moon with his two wings, its heart was broken, because it had been the equal of the light of the sun; so God, blessed and exalted, mended it with two things. The first of them: that He made the eyes look upon it in this world at the beginning of every month. The second: that He commanded His prophet Muḥammad — God bless him and grant him peace — to strike a similitude by it concerning the greatest and highest of things. If it be said: God, exalted is He, has said Eyes do not perceive Him, and He perceives the eyes (Q 6:103) — we say: we do not claim that the eyes perceive Him in the sense of encompassing Him; rather, what is attained /fol. 23v./ is the very act of looking, for the Maker, glorified and exalted, cannot admit of bounds. In the moon there are benefits. Among them: that it is a lamp for the creatures by night, and a miracle for our Prophet — God bless him and grant him peace — by His words, exalted is He: and the moon was split (Q 54:1). And He appointed for it mansions, that the appointed times might be known by them; and He effaced from its light 99 parts, by His words, exalted is He: so We effaced the sign of the night and made the sign of the day to give sight (Q 17:12). Were it not for that, people would have spread themselves abroad in their livelihoods by night and by day, and no one would have known night from day. And the Commander of the Faithful ʿAlī b. Abī Ṭālib — may God, exalted is He, ennoble his face — said that sleeping naked beneath the moon bequeaths leprosy; for a linen garment, when it is washed and hung out in the moonlight, rots before its time. And God, glorified and exalted, knows best what is right.
Faṣl: On the moon and its mansions

God, exalted is He, said: And the moon — We have determined mansions for it (Q 36:39). It is said that the mansions of the moon are 28 mansions, because each night the moon takes up its lodging in one of them. And their names are: al-Sharaṭayn, al-Buṭayn, al-Thurayyā, al-Dabarān, al-Haqʿa, al-Hanʿa, al-Dhirāʿ, al-Nathra, al-Ṭarf, al-Jabha, al-Zubra, al-Ṣarfa, al-Simāk, al-ʿAwwāʾ, al-Ghafr, al-Zubānā, al-Iklīl, al-Qalb, al-Shawla, al-Naʿāʾim, al-Balda, Saʿd al-Suʿūd, Saʿd Bulaʿ, Saʿd al-Dhābiḥ, Saʿd al-Akhbiya, Fargh al-Dalw al-Muqaddam, Fargh al-Dalw al-Muʾakhkhar, and al-Rishāʾ, which is al-Ḥūt (the Fish).
Faṣl: On the stars, what pertains to them, their indications, their determinations, and their mansions

God, exalted is He, said: And He it is who made the stars for you, that you might be guided by them through the darknesses of the land and the sea (Q 6:97). And He said, exalted is He: and by the star they are guided (Q 16:16). Saʿīd b. Jubayr related from Ibn ʿAbbās — may God, exalted is He, be pleased with them both — that he said: the science of the stars is a beneficial science, of which many people are incapable. By this he was pointing to the knowledge of the stars themselves, not to the astrological judgements. They agreed that the light of the moon is from the light of the sun, and they differed concerning the light of the [other] stars — whether it is from the light of the sun or from another light: on that there are two opinions. And that is because the known stars are 1,022 stars. Among them is al-Jady (the Kid, the pole star), which is the best of them for indicating the qibla. Al-Jady is a star beside the pole, by which the qibla is known. Al-Jady lies beside the northern pole, and around it are stars [forming] a circle like the farāsha (the pivot-plate) of a millstone; at one of its two ends are al-Farqadān, and at the other end a shining star facing them; and between it and that are small stars, three above and three below, which revolve about al-Jady and the pole as the pivot-plate of a millstone revolves about its spindle. Around it are Banāt Naʿsh, revolving about al-Jady and the pole — and these two do not stir from their place. One infers the pole only by al-Jady, and al-Jady is the pivot of this farāsha; though it is [also] said that the pole is its pivot, and that it is inferred by al-Jady when there is no moon. For when /fol. 24r./ the moon's light grows strong, its place is hidden, so that none sees it but the keen of sight.

Al-Suhā is at its side; it is a faint star by which people test their eyesight. And al-Jady, by which the qibla is known — it is the Jady of Banāt Naʿsh al-Ṣughrā (the Lesser Bier-daughters). Banāt Naʿsh al-Ṣughrā comes close to the Greater in the manner of its composition: four of them are the bier (naʿsh) and three are the daughters (banāt). Of the four are al-Farqadān, and they are the two that go in front; and of the daughters is al-Jady, and it is the last of them. And al-Suhā, by which people test their eyesight, is a faint star among Banāt Naʿsh; and it is said in the proverb: "I show her al-Suhā, and she shows me the moon." As for the manner of knowing the qibla by al-Jady: it is that you place it behind your back — in the land of Syria you would then be facing the qibla; while in the land of Iraq you place it opposite the back of your right ear, at the top of it, and you will then be facing the door of the House, toward the Maqām. And whenever you set your back to al-Farqadān or to Banāt
Naʿsh, you will be facing the direction of the Kaʿba. As for al-Farqadān, they are two shining stars close to the pole, and they are its boon-companions and its attendants.

I say: Banāt Naʿsh al-Kubrā are seven stars — four of them the bier and three the daughters — and so likewise are Banāt Naʿsh al-Ṣughrā. As for the northern pole, neither sun nor moon reaches it; and the southern pole is at the rising-place of Suhayl (Canopus); it does not appear except in the Arabian peninsula. Among them is Suhayl, which lies beside the southern pole. Its rising-place is from the quarter whence the south wind blows; then it travels toward the west and comes to stand in the qibla of the one who prays, and there it sets. Suhayl is a red star, standing apart from the [other] stars; and because of its nearness to the earth you see it as though it were throbbing. It is one of the Yamānī (southern) stars, and its rising-place is to the left of the qibla. It is seen throughout the whole land of the Arabs, from Iraq and from Syria, but it is not seen in the lands of Armenia; and between its rising in the Ḥijāz and its being seen in Iraq there are some ten-odd nights. Some of them have said that Suhayl is a star, and the Arabs say: "When Suhayl rises, do not feel safe from the flood." And it is said: "When Suhayl rises, the water grows cold and the night grows long."

Know that of these stars, which are 1,022 stars, there are 312 stars in 12 figures upon the path of the sun, and these are the twelve zodiacal signs. And of them there are 360 stars in 21 figures, which are those inclining away from the path of the sun toward the northern quarter; among them are the Greater Bear and the Lesser, and al-Tinnīn (the Dragon), and others. And of them there are 316 stars in 15 figures inclining away from the path of the sun toward the southern quarter. Reliance is placed upon the stars that lie on the path of the sun, because they are the belt of the zodiacal signs. As for those beyond the stars I have named, the generality of people have not named them, [but rather] the masters of the science of the celestial configuration (hayʾa); and Abū Muḥammad ʿAbd al-Jabbār, known as al-Ḥarmī, mentioned them in his book entitled al-Tabṣira fī l-kawākib al-thābita (The Elucidation, on the Fixed Stars). He said: As for the stars that are in the northern figures, among them is the Lesser Bear, which is in the shape of a bear standing and stretching out its tail. Its stars are seven, and the Arabs call them /fol. 24v./ Banāt Naʿsh al-Ṣughrā: four of them are the bier, in the shape of a square, and the three are upon the tip of its tail; and outside the figure there is one star. The one at the tip of its tail they call al-Jady, and it is the one by which the qibla is pointed out, since it is the nearest of the observed stars to the northern pole.

I say: among them is the Greater Bear, and its stars are 27 stars, while outside the figure there are eight stars of them; and among the whole of them are seven stars that the Arabs call Banāt Naʿsh al-Kubrā, four upon its forelegs and three upon its tail. The one at its tip they call al-Qāʾid (the Leader), then al-ʿAnāq, then al-Jawn; and near al-ʿAnāq is a small star which they call al-Suhā. Among them is al-Tinnīn, and it is 31 stars. Its figure is the figure of a great serpent with many coils, and it begins from four stars in the shape of a skewed square upon its head, which the Arabs call al-ʿAwāʾidh. Al-Tinnīn is a place in the north; and al-tinnīn is a kind of serpent, the greatest of them. Among them is al-Fakka, which is also called al-Iklīl al-Shamālī (the Northern Crown), and it is known as Qaṣʿat al-Masākīn (the beggars' bowl) because of its roundness; and its stars are eight. As for al-Fakka, [editor's gloss, garbled in the source: "…de la Lira. constelaci…gna a toda la constelaci…pios autores" — i.e. "…of the Lyre. …[some authors] assign [this name] to the whole constellation…"] it is a round [group of] stars behind al-Rāmiḥ. [Among them is] al-Jāthī ʿalā rukbatayhi (the Kneeler upon his knees), and its figure is 29 stars. Among them is al-Silbāq — it is also called al-Lūrā (the Lyre) and al-Ṣanj al-Rūmī (the Byzantine harp). Among them is al-Sulaḥfāt (the Tortoise), and its stars are ten; among their number is a brilliant star which they call al-Nasr al-Wāqiʿ (the Alighting Eagle), so named because its two wings are folded in. Among them are al-Nasr al-Ṭāʾir (the Flying Eagle) and al-Nasr al-Wāqiʿ. Among them is al-Dajāja (the Hen), which is 17 stars, with two stars outside the figure; and most of its stars are in the Milky Way, near al-Nasr al-Wāqiʿ.

Among them is Dhāt al-Kursī (the Lady of the Chair, Cassiopeia), 13 stars. Its figure is the figure of a woman seated upon a chair that has a back-rest, and she has let her legs hang down; and it lies in the very body of the Milky Way. Among its stars is al-Kaff al-Khaḍīb (the Dyed Hand), upon the face of the back-rest; it is known as Sanām al-Nāqa (the she-camel's hump). Among them is Barshāwush (Perseus), which is called Ḥāmil Raʾs al-Ghūl (the Bearer of the Head of the Ghoul); it is 26 stars, and those outside the figure are six stars, though three is the sounder [reckoning]. Its figure is the figure of a man standing upon his left leg, raising his right leg, his right hand above his head, and in his left hand a severed head, misshapen in form, called Raʾs al-Ghūl (the Head of the Ghoul). Among them is Mumsik al-ʿInān (the Holder of the Rein, Auriga), which is 24 stars. Its figure is the figure of a man standing, in one of his hands a whip, and his other hand gripping a rein, behind al-ʿAyyūq (Capella). Among them is al-Ḥawwāʾ (the Serpent-Bearer, Ophiuchus), which is 24 stars, and those outside the figure are five stars. Its figure is the figure of a man standing who has gripped a serpent with both his hands together. Among them is Ḥayyat al-Ḥawwāʾ (the Serpent of Ophiuchus), which is 28, gripped by al-Ḥawwāʾ; it has raised its head and its tail until its head rose on high. Among them is al-Sahm (the Arrow, Sagitta), which is five stars, like the beak of al-Dajāja (the Hen, Cygnus), and al-Nasr al-Wāqiʿ (the Alighting Eagle, Vega). Among them is al-ʿUqāb (the Eagle, Aquila), nine stars, and those outside the figure are six. Among its stars is al-Nasr al-Ṭāʾir (the Flying Eagle, Altair). Among them is al-Dulfīn (the Dolphin, Delphinus), which is ten stars gathered together behind al-Nasr al-Ṭāʾir. Its figure is the figure of a sea-creature resembling /fol. 25r./ an inflated skin-bag. Some of them have not mentioned it among the stars; the dolphin is rather a beast in the sea that rescues the drowning man. Among them is Qiṭʿat al-Faras (the Piece of the Horse, Equuleus), which is four stars; it is also called Muqaddam al-Faras (the Forepart of the Horse), behind the stars of al-Dulfīn. Among them is al-Faras al-Akbar (the Greater Horse, Pegasus) [editor's gloss, fragmentary and interrupting the phrase: "…horse] with wings … …ent like al-faras … …mage … …a height of its head … …a serpent"], which is Dhū al-Janāḥ (the Winged One); it is 20 stars, in the figure of a horse having a head and two forelegs, but having no hind legs and no rump. Among them is Andarūmīdā (Andromeda), which is also called al-Marʾa al-Musalsala (the Chained Woman), 22 stars. Its figure is the figure of a woman standing with her hand outstretched, in her hands a chain as though she were hung by it; and it is said that the chain is upon her legs. Among them is al-Muthallath (the Triangle, Triangulum), which is four stars, between the stars of al-Samaka (the Fish) and the bright star that is upon Raʾs al-Ghūl (Algol). The sum, then, of these northern figures is 360 stars.

As for the southern figures, their number is 310 stars. Among them is Qīṭus (Cetus), which is 22 stars. Its figure is the figure of a sea-creature having two legs, its tail like the tail of a whale. Among them is al-Jabbār (the Giant, Orion), 38 stars. Its figure is the figure of a man upon a chair, in his hand a staff, and about his waist a belt and a sword; and among its stars is Yad al-Jawzāʾ (the Hand of al-Jawzāʾ, Betelgeuse), which is a red star. Among them is al-Nahr (the River, Eridanus), which is 34 stars; its shape is the shape of a watercourse with many bends. Among them is al-Arnab (the Hare, Lepus), which is 12 stars gathered together beneath the foot of al-Jabbār, likened to a hare whose face is toward the west and whose hindquarters are toward the east. Among them is al-Kalb al-Akbar (the Greater Dog, Canis Major), which is 28 stars, and those outside the figure are 11 stars, behind the stars of al-Jawzāʾ and in front of al-Safīna (the Ship, Argo); among its stars is al-

Shiʿrā al-ʿAbūr (Sirius), a bright star, and it is called al-ʿAbūr, while the second is called al-Mirzam. Al-Shiʿrā is the star that rises after al-Jawzāʾ, and its rising falls in the severest heat. They are the two Shiʿrās: al-ʿAbūr, which is in al-Jawzāʾ, and al-Shiʿrā al-Ghumayṣāʾ (Procyon), which is in al-Dhirāʿ. The Arabs claim that the two are the sisters of Suhayl (Canopus). As for the two Mirzams, they are the Mirzams of the two Shiʿrās; they are two stars, one of them in al-Shiʿrā al-Shāmiyya (the northern Shiʿrā) and the other in al-Dhirāʿ. Among them is al-Kalb al-Aṣghar (the Lesser Dog, Canis Minor), which is two stars: one of them is called al-Shiʿrā al-Shāmiyya and [the other] al-Ghumayṣāʾ — two bright stars. Among them is al-Safīna (the Ship, Argo), 45 stars gathered in the southern quarter, which rise in the track of al-Kalb al-Akbar; among their number is Suhayl, the red star. Among them is al-Shujāʿ (the Serpent, Hydra), which is 25, and those outside the figure are two stars. Its figure is the figure of a long serpent with many coils; its head, made of four stars, has the form of a horse's face; it begins from Zubānā al-Sharaṭayn, and it lies between al-Shiʿrā al-Shāmiyya and Qalb al-Asad (Regulus). Among them is al-Kaʾs (the Cup, Crater), which is seven stars in a circular shape at the back of al-Shujāʿ, and [editor's gloss, fragmentary: "…ete was… …asad. …las, and it begins from zub[ānā]… (al-faras) …n… …of the fish"] it is called al-Bāṭiya (the Wine-bowl). Among them is al-Ghurāb (the Crow, Corvus), which is seven stars; it is called ʿArsh al-Simāk al-Aʿzal (the Throne of al-Simāk al-Aʿzal, Spica) [editor's gloss, fragmentary: "…star… …xa al-sim… …las that are called… …a circular figure upon the back of…"] and it is also called al-

Ḥibāʾ. Among them is Qanṭūrus (the Centaur, Centaurus), which is 37 stars. Its figure is the figure of an animal compounded of a man and a horse: its forepart is the forepart of a man, from his head to his back, and its hindpart is the hindpart of a horse, from the base of its back to its tail. /fol. 25v./ In his hand he has seized the legs of a beast of prey (sabʿ), and the Arabs call it Shamārīkh. Among them is al-Sabʿ (the Beast of Prey, Lupus), which is 19 stars gathered behind the stars of Qanṭūrus, along the southern flanks of al-ʿAqrab (Scorpio). Among them is al-Iklīl al-Janūbī (the Southern Crown, Corona Australis), 13 stars; their shape is the shape of a pine-cone, and its name is al-Qubba (the Dome) — and so the Arabs too call it. Among them is al-Ḥūt al-Janūbī (the Southern Fish, Piscis Austrinus), which is 11 stars, and those outside the figure are six stars. Its figure is a mighty fish; its stars lie to the south of the stars of al-Dalw (Aquarius), its head toward the east and its tail toward the west. Among them is the Milky Way (al-Majarra), to the south of the vertebrae (kharazāt) of al-ʿAqrab. This, then, is the sum of the southern and northern stars. I say: this which some of them have mentioned pertains specifically to the stars that are not well known. As for the seven planets and what comes under their heading, we shall mention them hereafter, if God, exalted is He, wills. And God, glorified be He, knows best.
Faṣl: On their bodies and what pertains to them

Know that the body of the Sun is the size of the world 160 and a half times; the body of the Moon is the size of the world 39 times, and likewise Venus (al-Zuhara), Mercury (ʿUṭārid), and Mars (al-Mirrīkh); the body of Jupiter (al-Mushtarī) is the measure of the world 82 times, and Jupiter is called al-Aḥwar (the bright-eyed one); and the body of Saturn (Zuḥal) is greater than the world by 99 times. Some of our learned men have said that the body of the Sun is 15 degrees before it and likewise behind it; the body of the Moon 12 degrees before it and likewise behind it; the body of Jupiter nine degrees before it and likewise behind it; and the body of Saturn the same; the body of Mars eight degrees before it and likewise behind it; the body of Venus seven degrees before it and likewise behind it; and the body of Mercury the same. And God knows best.

Know that every star in the heaven is the size of the world — and it is said, its measure many times over — save the Moon, for it is smaller than the earth. I say: as for the statement that the smallest star in the heaven is the size of the world, yes indeed; but as for what has been said concerning the Moon, no one has agreed with him upon it. As for the great fixed stars, they are al-Shiʿrā al-ʿAbūr, al-Simāk, al-Nasr al-Wāqiʿ, al-Nasr al-Ṭāʾir, Qalb al-Asad, and their like; and they are 15 stars. Each star of them is the size of the earth 94 and a half times.
Faṣl: On the traversal of the celestial spheres by the seven planets

Know that the Moon traverses the sphere in 29 days and less than a third of a day; Mercury traverses it in less than 28 days; Venus traverses it in 224 days and something more than two thirds of a day; the Sun traverses it in 365 days and something more than a quarter of a day; Mars traverses it in 630 days; Jupiter traverses it in 11 years and 327 days; and Saturn traverses the sphere in 29 Persian years and 176 days. /fol. 26r./ And God, glorified and exalted, knows best what is right.
Faṣl: On the sojourns of the planets in the zodiacal signs

Know that the Moon's sojourn in each sign is two nights and three nights; Mercury's sojourn in each sign is 15 days; Venus's sojourn in each sign is 25 days; the Sun's sojourn in each sign is a month; Mars's sojourn in each sign is 45 days; Jupiter's sojourn in each sign is a year; and Saturn's sojourn in each sign is 30 months. And God knows best.
Faṣl: On the exaltations of the planets

Know that the exaltation of the Moon is Taurus (al-Thawr); the exaltation of Mercury, Virgo (al-Sunbula); the exaltation of Venus, Pisces (al-Ḥūt); the exaltation of the Sun, Aries (al-Ḥamal); the exaltation of Mars, Capricorn (al-Jady); the exaltation of Jupiter, Cancer (al-Saraṭān); and the exaltation of Saturn, Libra (al-Mīzān).
Faṣl: On the Milky Way

It is said that it is a lamp in the heaven, because it is the gathering-place of the stars, like a dome; and it is the gate of heaven. The Arabs call it Umm al-Nujūm (the Mother of the Stars), because there is no patch in the heaven with a greater number of stars in it.
Faṣl: On what belongs to each planet of the seven days
Know that Sunday belongs to the Sun, Monday to the Moon, Tuesday to Mars, Wednesday to Mercury, Thursday to Jupiter, Friday to Venus, and Saturday to Saturn.
Faṣl: On the conjunction of the planets

The meaning of conjunction (qirān) is that the two planets come together in a single sign and thereupon exert an influence by the command of God, exalted is He, as He has wrought therein — so understand. When Saturn conjoins Jupiter, wars become general throughout the climes, and a king among the kings of the world dies. When Saturn conjoins Mars, it is as we have mentioned. When the Sun conjoins Saturn, it is likewise. When Venus conjoins Saturn, it indicates high prices and dearth. When Saturn conjoins Mercury, it indicates the prospering of the condition of the scribes. When Saturn conjoins the Moon, it indicates the appearance of injustice in judgements. When Jupiter conjoins Mars, the world meets with mighty hardships. And God knows best.
Faṣl: On the natures of the planets

Know that the Moon is feminine, cold, phlegmatic, and in it there is an accidental heat, because its light is from the light of the Sun. Its dominion is over the spleen and the lung, and it is a lesser benefic (saʿd aṣghar). Mercury is reckoned masculine and feminine; it is at one time benefic and at another malefic; heat and cold stand equal in its nature; and its dominion is speech and writing. Venus is feminine, of mixed temperament; she is a benefic, cold and moist; to her belongs phlegm; her dominion is over the pudenda and the joints; and to her belong appetite, the stringing of garlands, /fol. 26v./ the composing of melodies, singing, play, diversion, and laughter. The Sun is masculine, hot and dry; to it belongs yellow bile; it is benefic by aspect and malefic by opposition; its substance is gold; its dominion is over the heart; and to it belong eminence, elevation, joy, gladness, and kingship. Mars is feminine, fiery, hot and dry, a malefic; to it belongs yellow bile; its substance is iron; its taste is bitter; its dominion is over the head and the stomach; and to it belong the deadly disease, slaying, and the ruin of women in pregnancy. And Jupiter is masculine, temperate, spiritual, airy, a benefic; to it belongs blood; and its substance is tin.

Its taste is sweet and its colour white; its dominion is over the wind that dwells in the heart; and to it belong bounty, worship, elevation, and leadership. Saturn is masculine, cold, dry, and dark; to it belongs the black bile; its substance is lead; its taste is bitter and its colour black; its dominion is over the male members; and to it belong boldness, singularity, solitude, subjugation, and tyrannical might. And God knows best.

I say: a party have claimed that these zodiacal signs, the celestial spheres, and the wandering planets exert the influence within the world, and that it is they that govern the worlds; and they argued from His words, exalted is He: and those that govern an affair (Q 79:5), and the like. But we say: it has been transmitted that Idrīs — peace be upon him — when he ascended to heaven, was given knowledge of the zodiacal signs, of the stars, and of other things besides these two. So whatever has come from him in this matter is accepted, and whatever the Law has forbidden is not to be regarded. Rather, the demonstrations and the indications have been established, [showing] that the Maker (al-Bāriʾ), glorified and exalted, invented them, brought them into being, and originated them. As for His words and those that govern an affair (Q 79:5), Ibn ʿAbbās said: they are the angels — some of them charged with the provisions, some charged with the rain, and some charged with the winds, according to what is mentioned in [the account of] the creation of the angels. And even if they were governors, it would be by the leave of the Maker, mighty and exalted; for He is al-Qādir (the Powerful), al-ʿAlīm (the Knowing), al-Mudabbir (the Governor), al-Ḥakīm (the
Wise), glorified and exalted. So glory be to Him whose power this power is and whose wisdom this wisdom is! Truly, His is the creation and the command. Blessed be God, Lord of the Worlds (Q 7:54).

The Letters of the Zodiac Signs
Manbaʿ Uṣūl al-Ḥikma, vol. I, p. 27
[I 28] The Qualities of the Zodiac Signs Aries, Leo and Sagittarius are dry and hot in nature. These three signs are called the fiery triplicity (musellesati nariye).
Taurus, Virgo and Capricorn are dry and cold in nature. These three signs are called the earthy triplicity (musellesati turabiye).
Gemini, Libra and Aquarius are moist and hot in nature. These three signs are called the airy triplicity (musellesati havaiye).
Cancer, Scorpio and Pisces are moist and cold in nature. These three signs are called the watery triplicity (musellesati maiye).
Aries, Cancer, Libra and Capricorn are called the cardinal signs (burucu munkalibe, "turning signs").
Taurus, Leo, Scorpio and Aquarius are called the fixed signs (burucu sabite, "standing signs").
Gemini, Virgo, Sagittarius and Pisces are called the mutable signs (burucu mumtezij, "mixed signs").
Aries, Gemini, Leo, Libra, Sagittarius and Aquarius are reckoned masculine and diurnal.
Taurus, Cancer, Virgo, Scorpio, Capricorn and Pisces are reckoned feminine and nocturnal.
Aries, Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, Leo and Virgo are called the northern signs (burucu shimaliye).
Libra, Scorpio, Sagittarius, Capricorn, Aquarius and Pisces are called the southern signs (burucu cenubiye).
The Months of the Zodiac Signs
Manbaʿ Uṣūl al-Ḥikma, vol. I, p. 28
According to a person's birth date, the sign to which they belong and [I 29] the months belonging to that sign are set out below in the following order.
Those born between March and April belong to Aries.
Those born between April and May belong to Taurus.
Those born between May and June belong to Gemini.
Those born between June and July belong to Cancer.
Those born between July and August belong to Leo.
Those born between August and September belong to Virgo.
Those born between September and October belong to Libra.
Those born between October and November belong to Scorpio.
Those born between November and December belong to Sagittarius.
Those born between December and January belong to Capricorn.
Those born between January and February belong to Aquarius.
Those born between February and March belong to Pisces.

[I 37] The Secret of the Letters The letters hold many secrets, and these secrets can be known by none but the righteous and chosen servants to whom Allah, Glorified and Exalted, has granted this knowledge.

The science of basṭ (yaymak, "to spread" or "expand") and taksir (jhoghaltmak, "to multiply" or "increase") is noble, of great worth, and highly beneficial. Through this science benefits are drawn near and harms are driven away; whatever is desired is obtained by the permission of Allah, the Exalted. This is a hidden treasure, and there are three distinct ways of employing the letters: by numerals, by letters, and by number-words.
1. The basṭof numerals: substituting each letter, as it stands, according to its own numerical value is called "the basṭof numerals" (Rakam basti). For example:
Lam, Kāf, Ye, Ṭāʾ, Ha, Ze, Wāw, He, Dal, Jīm, Be, Alif.
2. The basṭof letters: substituting each letter by pronouncing its name exactly as it is spoken is called "the basṭof letters" (Ḥarf basti). For example:
Za', Wāw, Ha', Dal, Jīm, Ba', Alif.
3. The basṭof number-words: converting each letter's numerical value into a written-out number-word and substituting that is called "the basṭ of number-words" (Adet basti). For example:
